route.name: Traditional
route.whatItIs: The client's design team completes the design; contractors then price and build it. The client keeps design control.
route.bestWhen: Design can be completed before tender; cost certainty and design quality matter more than speed.
route.watchOuts: Slowest route to site. Gaps in the design become client variations. Little contractor input to buildability.

model.name: Lump sum
model.whatItIs: One agreed price for a defined scope; the contractor carries the risk of its own pricing.
model.bestWhen: Scope and design are well defined and the client wants a firm price at award.
model.watchOuts: Unclear or changing scope leads to variations and claims. Contractors add risk allowances where information is poor.

contract.jct: JCT Intermediate (IC); ICD where the contractor designs part (e.g. M&E)
contract.nec4: ECC Option A (priced contract with activity schedule); ECSC for simple low-value work
contract.notes: Tender on a full specification or bills of quantities.

routeToMarket.name: Framework — direct award
routeToMarket.whatItIs: Direct appointment of one framework contractor, where the framework rules allow.
routeToMarket.bestWhen: Speed is critical, or early engagement with a proven contractor is needed (often with two-stage).
routeToMarket.watchOuts: Public and eligible bodies only. Less price competition — needs a strong cost consultant. Must follow the framework's award rules.

route.name: Two-stage (PCSA)
route.whatItIs: A contractor is appointed early under a pre-construction services agreement on fees and prelims, helps develop the design, then prices the works open-book for the second stage.
route.bestWhen: Complex, occupied or phased work, or poor existing information, where early contractor input to sequencing and buildability pays off.
route.watchOuts: Less price competition at the second stage. Needs a strong cost consultant to test the price. Scope creep if not controlled.

model.name: Lump sum
model.whatItIs: One agreed price for a defined scope; the contractor carries the risk of its own pricing.
model.bestWhen: Scope and design are well defined and the client wants a firm price at award.
model.watchOuts: Unclear or changing scope leads to variations and claims. Contractors add risk allowances where information is poor.

contract.jct: JCT Pre-Construction Services Agreement (PCSA), then JCT DB (or SBC)
contract.nec4: First stage under NEC4 Professional Service Contract (PSC); construction under ECC Option A
contract.notes: Test the second-stage price against benchmarks before signing.

routeToMarket.name: Selective tender
routeToMarket.whatItIs: A shortlist of 4–6 suitable contractors is invited to tender.
routeToMarket.bestWhen: The client wants competition among contractors of proven capability.
routeToMarket.watchOuts: Public bodies above the threshold need a compliant procedure (e.g. competitive flexible) to shortlist. Prequalification takes time.

aiProse.executiveSummary: This report assesses the refurbishment of Hargreaves Teaching Block, a three-storey 1960s education building at Example University, Birmingham, totalling 1200 m² GIFA. The project will replace life-expired heating, ventilation and electrical services, upgrade fire safety, and improve thermal performance to support net-zero objectives. The estimated project cost is £2,150,000 to £3,159,000 excluding VAT, with Grade C (Limited Confidence) due to early design stage and absence of an asbestos refurbishment survey. The target date of 1 September 2028 is achievable. The single most material risk is asbestos removal during strip-out, which may extend programme and cost if finds occur.
keyFindings: The works cost mid-point is £1,507,000 (range £1,281,000–£1,884,000), with construction duration of 26 weeks and total programme of 77 weeks including design and surveys.
The target date of 1 September 2028 is achievable from a start of 11 January 2027, with approximately 9 weeks of programme buffer.
The stated budget of £4,500,000 including fees and VAT is sufficient against the estimated gross range, with headroom of approximately £709,000 above the top of the range.
The most significant survey gap is the absence of a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey; asbestos removal is priced but the scope and cost remain uncertain until survey reports.
The preferred option for the client to consider is a Traditional procurement route with lump-sum pricing, which offers design control and cost certainty where design can be completed before tender.
scopeAssumptions: External plant space for the air source heat pump is included within the heating and hot water scope.
The building has 18 standard WCs and 3 accessible WCs being refurbished as part of the full systems replacement.
All 20 scope items covering structure, services, finishes and compliance are being costed; no items are excluded or assumed complete.
aiProse.costNarrative: The works cost reflects full replacement of heating, ventilation, electrical and water services across the entire building, together with asbestos removal, strip-out, windows, doors, fire stopping and all finishes. Preliminaries are elevated by partial occupation, restricted working hours, complex services and a hard deadline. Professional fees reflect early design stage and M&E complexity, with a risk allowance of 16% to cover design development, construction uncertainty and the absence of an asbestos survey.
aiProse.roiNarrative: The project cost mid-point is £2,526,000 with an annual operational benefit of £95,000, giving a simple payback of 26.6 years. The key financial risk is that energy savings may not materialise if the building's actual energy performance in use falls short of design assumptions, or if utility costs do not rise as forecast.

constraints.title: Vacation-only working
constraints.text: Works must be confined to academic vacation windows, avoiding examination periods in January and May–June, which constrains programme flexibility and may extend duration.

constraints.title: Restricted working hours
constraints.text: Limited working hours on a single service road in the middle of campus will increase preliminary costs and may require out-of-hours working to maintain programme.

constraints.title: Conservation area
constraints.text: The site is in a conservation area; external alterations will likely require full planning consent with enhanced materials and detailing.

constraints.title: Asbestos uncertainty
constraints.text: Asbestos is known or suspected; licensed removal, notification and air testing add cost and time, and finds during strip-out may stop work.

nextSteps: Commission a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey immediately to confirm scope and cost of removal before Stage 2 design begins.
Confirm with the university which academic vacation windows are available for construction, and agree blackout dates to avoid examination periods.
Engage the conservation officer for pre-application advice on external alterations, materials and detailing to avoid delays at planning.
Instruct an M&E condition and capacity survey at Stage 2 to verify the scope of service replacement and confirm electrical supply capacity with the DNO.
Develop a phasing strategy at Stage 2 to minimise disruption to teaching, and confirm whether long-lead procurement of major plant (switchgear, AHUs) is viable to accelerate the critical path.

riskRegister.description: Works confined to vacation windows; programme spans multiple academic terms; risk of overrun into term time.
riskRegister.mitigation: Phase works to vacation windows; agree blackout dates with faculty; build programme float; consider out-of-hours working.

riskRegister.description: Restricted working hours extend construction duration and may attract premium or out-of-hours rates.
riskRegister.mitigation: Confirm permitted hours with the client; price out-of-hours working where programme-critical; reflect in Prelims.

riskRegister.description: Ageing or inadequate mechanical and electrical services: capacity, condition and compliance of existing plant and distribution are uncertain and may need more replacement than assumed.
riskRegister.mitigation: Commission an M&E condition and capacity survey at Stage 2; confirm supply capacity with the utility early.

riskRegister.description: Asbestos is known or suspected: licensed removal, notification periods and air testing add cost and time, and finds during strip-out can stop work.
riskRegister.mitigation: Commission a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey before Stage 2 design; carry a provisional sum for removal until it reports.

riskRegister.description: Site is in a conservation area or under an Article 4 direction: external alterations are likely to need full planning, with enhanced materials and detailing.
riskRegister.mitigation: Seek pre-application advice from the conservation officer; assume full planning for external works; allow for enhanced materials when costing.

riskRegister.description: Heating and hot water: electrical capacity and DNO check required for air source heat pump installation.
riskRegister.mitigation: Investigate and confirm during Stage 2 design, and carry the outcome into the cost plan.

riskRegister.description: Design at Stage 0–1 introduces uncertainty in specification, buildability and cost; risk allowance of 16% reflects this.
riskRegister.mitigation: Progress design rapidly to Stage 2; engage cost consultant and contractor input on buildability and sequencing.

riskRegister.description: Multiple phasing strategy with partial occupation during works increases coordination complexity and risk of disruption.
riskRegister.mitigation: Confirm phase split and occupation strategy at Stage 2; agree detailed sequencing and liaison protocols with faculty.

aiProse.procurementNarrative: The traditional route with lump-sum pricing and framework direct award suits this project because design can be completed before tender, cost certainty matters to the client, and the framework rules allow direct appointment of a proven contractor. Alternatively, a two-stage approach with selective tender would be better if early contractor input to sequencing and buildability in this occupied, phased building proves essential to managing disruption and risk.
procurementConsiderations: Gaps in the design at Stage 0–1 may lead to variations and claims; ensure the specification is detailed before tender.
Direct award to a framework contractor reduces price competition; a strong cost consultant must test the price against benchmarks.
Scope creep in a two-stage route needs tight control; the alternative requires testing the second-stage price before signing.
procurementConflicts: Traditional lump-sum pricing offers cost certainty but requires design completion before tender, which may delay site start.
